questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere where I knew the culture was different from the one in Denmark. I also wanted to go somewhere where the range of courses on offer was quite different, so that I could broaden my academic profile. Milan is, in many ways, less ‘Italian’ than most of Italy, so I was also aware that it would be a city offering many opportunities, socially, culturally and academically. I knew the city was international, which meant I would automatically meet people of many different nationalities and find myself in a city that is used to welcoming people from all over the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Milan is an expensive city, and as there are many exchange students arriving every semester, you need to be prepared to pay high rent. The university finds it difficult to help with accommodation, as there are too many people competing for it.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: My immediate impression was that communication from UNIMI was good, they often replied quickly and also have a physical office for Erasmus students, which you can visit as and when needed. The Italian university system is different from the Danish one, and on several occasions I felt there was a lack of proper guidance and communication regarding courses, enrolment, exams, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was given a bit of guidance on the need to visit their Erasmus office to collect my student ID card and other information. However, I found that I ended up seeking information myself or turning up for lectures and asking lecturers and students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I feel that I ended up being responsible for finding answers to several questions and had to seek out the information myself.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: The housing situation in Milan is very similar to that in Copenhagen, which is why it’s incredibly challenging to find a good place to live at a reasonable price. I ended up doing so through an agency where I knew they would not trick me. However, I paid an incredibly high rent. That said, this included a good location, a large room, air conditioning and a balcony, which is well worth the money, especially during the hot months at the summer. I was also sharing with five other people, though, which I didn’t feel made it any cheaper.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
You need to be prepared to pay a lot of money for accommodation down here. Of course, there are cheaper areas, but you have to weigh this up against the location and other factors. Many people share accommodation, as it works out cheaper.
Be wary of scams. My impression is that many people use property portals here. However, I also know that people take advantage of the fact that students are willing to pay quite a lot of money for accommodation, etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn’t live in student accommodation, but shared a flat with five other students.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The process for registering for courses is quite different from that at KU, and I found I had to figure it out for myself to some extent. However, the courses aren’t tied in the same way, nor are the exams, so it didn’t matter too much that I didn’t have a proper grasp of it at the start.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You enrol on courses via the UNIMIA website, where you add them to your study plan, and then you can find the course on ARIEL, where you can view timetables and so on, a bit like Absalon at the University of Copenhagen. You can view the courses in the course catalogue on the UNIMIA website.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I asked both teachers and students for help with registration and so on. I also think the Erasmus Office might be able to offer some guidance on this.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Particularly during my first term down here (the second term, January–March), there were quite a few more courses on offer and I managed to get into everything I wanted. In the third term, it was harder to find any that were relevant, and they filled up more quickly as more students had joined from March onwards.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try attending the courses to see if they’re right for you, and do think about which semester you’ll be attending them in. Sometimes the lecturers would look at the number of people signed up and say the course was full, but try to speak to the lecturers whenever possible.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The standard was probably a little lower overall compared to KU, but the way the exams were conducted – with so much of it done without aids and by hand – meant that my exam readings were more difficult.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I definitely felt that, in some modules, the standard and expectations were lower. However, I had other modules where they were very demanding and required us to gather empirical data in our spare time and produce a short BA thesis as the final project. Both the teaching and the exams differed, as some involved a great deal of active participation, with ongoing projects or tests that you had to pass. Others were more like lectures and involved either a final written assignment or an oral component as well. A lot of the work was done by hand and without aids, which is something you need to be prepared for.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Sociology of Globalization, Consumer Culture, Visual Communication, Ethical theory and hard choices.

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Visual communication & Consumer culture, as they, in particular, introduced me to a new and specialised field within sociology, which I had not been exposed to at the University of Copenhagen.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Supermarkets are generally quite expensive in Milan, so shopping turned out to be a bigger expense than expected. Some items are cheaper than in Denmark, but many are at the same price level.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport is definitely cheaper than in Denmark. In addition, there were lots of free events to take part in. Eating out is also cheaper in most places than in Copenhagen, but because Milan is a big city, food is often on the pricey side; however, drinks are quite a bit cheaper in restaurants and bars than in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: ESN in Milan organises loads of free events, although the best ones require an ESN card; however, it’s well worth the money when you can get into museums, La Scala and so on.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: With an Esn card, you could take part in many cultural activities, such as visits to museums, the ballet, sport, and so on. In addition, Milan hosts many free events in the city, such as Fashion Week, Design Week, the Piano Festival, markets, and so on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend going out to see Design Week, the piano festival, the markets and the open-air concerts.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Milan is close to many lovely towns and areas, so go out and explore Italy, go for a swim in the lakes, and so on. There are good transport links by train, bus and plane, so go and explore.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I haven’t learnt much Italian, as Milan is a big city and many of the people living here aren’t Italian. However, I think you should try to find the traditional restaurants, cafés, bars and so on, and soak up the atmosphere. If you know where the Italians themselves go, then go there. I find that you’re made to feel very welcome and that they’re an open-minded people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: By taking part in ESN events, you automatically met some Italians. However, I found it a bit difficult to make friends with them. You just have to pluck up the courage to talk to people in class and others you meet along the way. Often, they’ll also be keen to learn about your culture, so a good way to do this is to share your own culture and home country.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In Denmark, we tend to want everything to happen quite quickly, and it’s definitely not like that down here. I’ve found it a bit difficult to cope with long response times, meetings running over, and so on, but you learn as you go along.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I thought people were very welcoming and in good spirits. That slower pace of life is just what Italy is all about. We could learn a lot from that and from their wonderful culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: You’ll sort it all out in the end, and it doesn’t need to be all sorted before you get here. The system is different and the courses are different. However, you won’t be registered for the exam until just before it takes place, so just relax. It’ll all work out. Don’t be afraid to ask students or teachers for help

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: UNIMI is a bit like the University of Copenhagen, so there are several faculties and different addresses depending on where your classes are held. Make sure you’ve got a good grasp of this so you know where you need to be. The venues are in different parts of the city.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Having the courage to take the plunge into something new, step outside your comfort zone, and get to know new people, cultures and fields. It’s never a waste of time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out the system and having the courage to let go of control.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
